title: Media Ownership
blurb: Concentration, regulation and the platforms: parliament on the press.

brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about media ownership?
brief.answer:
The parliamentary record shows Australian Labor Party members consistently argued that cross-media ownership rules, introduced in 1987–88 under Paul Keating, were essential to protect democracy and were under sustained attack by the Howard government. Speakers cited concentration statistics to justify retaining the rules: News Ltd controlled around two-thirds of capital city and national newspapers, three-quarters of Sunday newspapers and nearly half the suburban newspaper market, while Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd controlled the Nine network, three metropolitan and one regional television licence reaching more than half the potential audience, 65 magazines, and online operations including ninemsn. One speaker reported that 80 per cent of Australians opposed further concentration of media ownership, and that 88 per cent of Australians used free-to-air television, 76 per cent radio and 76 per cent newspapers as news sources, compared with only 10 per cent for pay TV and 11 per cent for the internet.

The debate shifted from the Broadcasting Services Amendment (Media Ownership) Bill 2002 to a further bill in 2006, but Labor's core critique remained the same: the government wanted to let one proprietor own newspapers, television and radio in the same market. In 2002, Senator Alston argued that "ownership of media per se is irrelevant" and that a "plethora of sources" made old rules redundant. By 2006, Senator Coonan was reported to have flagged allowing newspaper proprietors to own television, radio, monopoly pay TV and internet interests. Labor speakers quoted earlier statements by government frontbenchers—including the member for Hinkler in 1995 and the member for Bradfield in 1997—warning against media concentration, and accused those members of hypocrisy for supporting the later bills. Labor also suggested that rather than relaxing cross-media rules, the government should relax foreign ownership restrictions to bring in new competitors.

The sharpest disagreement was over whether ownership actually controls media content. Government spokesmen claimed that separate editorial processes could protect diversity and that ownership was not the key issue. Labor responded with the maxim "he who pays the piper calls the tune," arguing that proprietors ultimately determine what is published or broadcast, and that an editorial separation test administered by the Australian Broadcasting Authority—whose chairman, Professor David Flint, had argued that journalist independence outweighs ownership—was inadequate. Speakers also accused the government of acting on behalf of Rupert Murdoch and Kerry Packer, with one Labor member calling the 2006 bill part of a "dirty" deal between Prime Minister Howard and Packer to destroy the cross-media laws, and describing the result as the most concentrated media ownership in Australian history.

The government's public promise was that the changes would preserve local news and separate editorial voices: the Prime Minister's answer to a question on notice said exemptions from cross-media rules would be granted if companies maintained existing levels of locally produced news and current affairs and put in place separate editorial processes. Opposition speakers dismissed this as nonsense, noting that the bill allowed a proprietor to own a dominant newspaper, television station and radio stations in the same market, and warning of scenarios where PBL could buy Fairfax or News Corp could take over a free-to-air network. Labor claimed the real outcome would be three huge conglomerates based around the commercial television networks, reduced newsroom independence and fewer journalists willing to criticise their employers, with one speaker warning that the legislation would hand media owners influence over future elections.

positions.position: Opposes further concentration of power in television and newspapers, arguing democracy works best with a strong and diverse media. Supports an independent view on diversity of voices in one of the most concentrated media markets in the world, and opposed removing the two-out-of-three cross-media ownership rule warning it would increase media concentration.

positions.position: Supports a 'two out of three' rule for media mergers in metropolitan and regional areas as an additional safeguard against undue media concentration.

sections.question: What have MPs said about media ownership concentration in Australia?
sections.answer: MPs—mainly from the opposition and crossbench—have strongly criticized media ownership concentration in Australia, saying it threatens democracy and the public interest. They argued that further concentration would reduce media diversity, stifle competition, and give too much power to major proprietors like Rupert Murdoch and James Packer. They also noted that Australia has one of the most concentrated media landscapes in the Western world, with News Limited and Fairfax dominating the news industry. Some MPs accused government frontbenchers of hypocrisy, saying those MPs had opposed concentration when they were backbenchers but later supported or remained silent on bills that would allow greater concentration. They also highlighted specific risks, such as allowing one company to own television, radio, and newspapers in the same market, and called for retaining cross-media ownership rules to protect democracy.

sections.question: What was said about the news media bargaining code and tech platforms?
sections.answer: Based on the provided context, the news media bargaining code was described as a world-first mandatory code to address bargaining power imbalances between major digital platforms—such as Google and Facebook—and Australian news media businesses. It was established to ensure digital platforms pay Australian news media for using their content, especially public interest journalism. The code's framework includes good-faith bargaining, compulsory arbitration, notification of algorithm changes, non-differentiation, allowing commercial deals outside the code, and standard offers. It also uses a negotiate-arbitrate model, with the Treasurer able to designate platforms based on ACCC advice, and includes provisions for small and regional publishers. The need for the code was based on ACCC findings that digital platforms had substantial bargaining power over news businesses. There was bipartisan support in principle, but also criticism of government delays and concerns about impacts on small businesses, media diversity, and uncertainty about designations. Recent commercial deals between Google and companies like Seven, Nine, News Corp, and Junkee Media were cited as evidence the code was encouraging commercial negotiations.
